newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge aims to stop leaks in Ruiz Massieu case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge aims to stop leaks in Ruiz Massieu case.

text.p: A U.S. judge on Tuesday moved to stop news leaks in the case of a former Mexican deputy attorney general whom the United States government has accused of taking money from drug traffickers.

The action followed publication in Mexico over the weekend of documents that linked former prosecutor Mario Ruiz Massieu, former Mexican President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, his brother Raul and other officials to drug traffickers.

U.S. District Judge Nancy Atlas ruled in a hearing that from now until the Ruiz Massieu trial, lawyers from both sides would not be allowed copies of sensitive information gathered during the pre-trial discovery process. She said that by not having copies floating around, leaks would be avoided.

Ruiz Massieu was set to go to trial on March 10 in a civil proceeding in which the United States government is trying to confiscate more than $9 million from his Houston bank account on grounds that it came from drug-related bribes.
Atlas' unusual ruling came after a request by prosecutors to sanction Ruiz Massieu's attorney, Tony Canales, whom they accused of leaking the information published by the Mexican magazine Proceso.

Proceso said government witnesses had implicated Ruiz Massieu, the Salinas brothers and their father, and two assassinated political leaders, Luis Donaldo Colosio and Francisco Ruiz Massieu, in an operation that took millions of dollars in bribes from drug traffickers, in exchange for protection. Franciso Ruiz Massieu was Mario's brother.
The Salinas brothers denied the allegations on Monday.
Prosecutor Susan Kempner said the release of the information had put the government's witnesses in danger. "One of my witnesses doesn't want to proceed," she said.
Canales denied he leaked the information, which included the government's written responses to his questions about their case, and said officials in Mexico were responsible.
Atlas said she would not yet rule on the government's request for sanctions against Canales.

Ruiz Massieu was assigned by then-President Salinas to investigate the death of his brother, who was the head of Mexico's ruling party when he was gunned down on a Mexico City street in September 1994. He stunned the country by blaming the killing on old-guard political forces.

But he fled Mexico when prosecutors charged him with drug-related corruption. He was arrested in the United States and is currently under house arrest in New Jersey. Attempts to extradite him to Mexico have been turned down by U.S. judges because of a lack of evidence against him.
